I had plenty of free time to do that and I was really motivated to have a healthy lifestyle. After the summer of 2018, I had to move out to another city and live alone. I couldn’t make any friends there, I felt extremely alone on some days and, apart from that, I hated what I was studying at college. I didn’t know how to handle these endless moments of loneliness (combined with a and I just started to eat a lot as a coping mechanism: I ate 4-5 times a day, fast-food every week and an exaggerated amount of sweets and chocolate daily. There’s no wonder I’ve gained around 10 kilos in less than 6 months. I feel very guilty for this and I wish I had motivation and energy for going to the gym, but I feel so tired every day. WIBTA for telling me he’s a jerk and he should stop with this bullshit because it affects me? I know fat acceptance is a bullshit and you shouldn’t encourage someone to tolerate their harmful lifestyle, but it does affect me.

For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. You’ve got this! If she’s **defending him** or **ignoring it**, that’s a red flag about her own boundaries. A healthy sister would **protect you** from toxic behavior, not enable it. 3. **The "But I’m Guilty" Trap** - You say you feel **guilty** for gaining weight, but **guilt doesn’t lead to change**—**compassion does**. His criticism **feeds your shame**, which is counterproductive. If you want to improve your health, **you need support, not punishment**. 4. **Is "Jerk" the Right Word?** - Calling someone a "jerk" is **emotionally charged**. If you want to **de-escalate**, you could say: *"That’s not helpful. I’m struggling, and I’d rather talk about solutions than hear criticism."* If he **still** doesn’t change, then yes, "jerk" is fair. --- ### **What Would I Do?** 1. **Start with a boundary** (not an attack): *"I know you mean well, but your questions about my weight are making me feel bad. I’d rather focus on how I can improve *with* support, not *because* of judgment."* - If he **listens**, great. If he **doubles down**, then: 2. **Call him out directly** (if safe): *"You’re being a jerk. My body isn’t a project for you to critique. If you care about me, you’d talk to me like a person, not a problem."* - This is **<1>**—justified because his behavior is **toxic**. 3. **Document & Reflect** - If this is **part of a pattern**, consider whether this relationship is **healthy for you**. Toxic criticism from loved ones can **erode self-worth**. 4. **Focus on Your Health (Not His Criticism)** - If you **want** to improve, **you’re the one who decides how**. His criticism **won’t motivate you**—**self-compassion will**. Try: - **Small, sustainable changes** (e.g., one healthy meal a day, walking instead of gym). - **Therapy or support groups** for loneliness/depression (this is **why** you’re eating, not "laziness"). - **Body-neutrality exercises** (e.g., *"I’m not my weight"* mantras). --- ### **Final Verdict: <1> (Yes, You’d Be Justified)** But with **important context**: - **If he’s a one-time critic** → A firm *"Stop"* or *"That’s not okay"* is enough. - **If he’s a pattern** → Calling him a "jerk" is **not justifiable**—it’s **necessary** to protect your mental health. - **The bigger issue** isn’t whether you say "jerk"—it’s whether **he changes**.
